e.t: Abed, also rendered Aveth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. This name occurs once in the LXX, in Nehemiah 12:20. Without the surrounding verse text, Scripture does not provide enough here to explain more about the person or the significance of the name. Its basic meaning is therefore the personal designation “Abed” or “Aveth.”

This Greek LXX verb means “indignant”: it describes becoming upset, displeased, or angered by something considered wrong or offensive. It expresses a strong inward reaction rather than a calm judgment. The word appears three times in the LXX corpus represented here, in Wisdom and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on what provokes the reaction and how the surrounding sentence presents it.

Aimath, also rendered Emath, is a proper name used for a place in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies a location named in the biblical record. The name occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 12 verses, from 2 Kings through Jeremiah. Its exact significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and its mention there.

This adjective means “unveiled,” describing something that is not covered or concealed. It refers to an uncovered condition rather than naming an action or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Leviticus 13:45. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense remains plainly visible: something is exposed instead of covered. This word belongs to the Greek LXX vocabulary and should be understood within that corpus.

Alemōni, also given as Alemoni, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 21:3. Its available lexical information identifies it as a name but does not provide a broader descriptive meaning. Therefore, it should be understood as a name used in that passage, while the precise role it plays depends on the surrounding verse context.

This is a proper name rendered “Hamathitis” or “Amathitis.” It identifies a named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 12:25. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, its precise reference in that passage cannot be described further. The two approved renderings preserve the name in slightly different forms, but both point to the same lexical designation.

This Greek LXX noun means “cousin,” referring to a family member related through the wider family rather than an immediate sibling. It is used once in the Greek LXX, at Numbers 36:11, and its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. The word identifies a person’s family relationship; the exact significance of that relationship in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word means “opponent”: someone who stands against another person or party. It can function as a noun for the opposing person or as an adjective describing someone or something opposed. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times, including passages involving people who resist, contend with, or stand against others. Its basic sense is therefore a person or side in opposition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific conflict or situation intended.

This verb means “hated” or “incur hatred.” It describes being the object of hatred or becoming hateful to others, depending on how the sentence uses it. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 2:30. The word therefore expresses a relationship of hostility or deep aversion, but the precise force in that single passage depends on the surrounding verse text.

The word means “revelation,” referring to something revealed or made known. As a noun, it names the reality or act of revelation rather than describing a person or action directly. In this Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 19 times, with most occurrences in Leviticus 18. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, which is not included here. This remains a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that corpus.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut off” or “sever”—to separate something by cutting it away. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word appears four times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Jeremiah, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on what is being separated and the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains decisive cutting or removal.

gl: of free choice; of one’s own accord
d: of free choice; of one’s own accord

e.t: This adverb describes something done by free choice or by one’s own accord. It emphasizes voluntary action rather than compulsion, pressure, or mere accident. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its basic force is to show that a person acts willingly and personally, taking the initiative for the action. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what action is being described, but the word itself highlights willing participation.

gl: separate offering; that which is set apart
d: separate offering; that which is set apart

e.t: This noun means “a separate offering” or “that which is set apart.” It refers to something distinguished from ordinary use and dedicated as an offering. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times, all in Ezekiel. The word therefore centers on an offering marked off for a special purpose, rather than something common or unrestricted. Its exact force in any verse is clarified by the surrounding passage.

“Baalim” or “Vaalim” is a proper name used to identify a named subject in the Greek Old Testament. It is not an ordinary description of an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 16 times, from Judges through Hosea, and is especially found in passages recorded in Judges and Hosea. Because the available lexical definition gives only the name itself, its precise reference in any particular verse must be understood from that passage’s surrounding context.

Barouch, also rendered Varukh, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek LXX tradition. The name occurs 26 times in this LXX corpus, especially in Jeremiah, and also appears in Nehemiah and Baruch. Its significance in any particular passage comes from the person being named and the surrounding context, not from a separate common-word meaning.

This word means to “intend” or “deliberate”—to form a purpose, make plans, or decide what one will do. As a verb, it describes purposeful thinking or planning rather than a merely accidental action. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings, it occurs 80 times, showing that it can describe both private intentions and decisions made with others. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on planning, resolving, or choosing a course of action.

Gader is a proper name rendered “Gader,” with “Gather” also given as a meaning form. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, once in Genesis and once in Joshua. Because it functions as a name rather than an ordinary descriptive word, its main role is to identify a particular named place or entity in those passages. The exact reference depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

This noun means a treasury—a place where money, valuables, or dedicated offerings are kept. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it refers to a storage place rather than to the wealth itself. The word occurs 22 times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages concerning temple and administrative treasuries. Its basic sense remains consistent whether referring to one treasury or several. The surrounding verse determines what specific goods or funds are being stored there.

This Greek LXX verb means “father” or “born.” It describes the act of a man becoming the father of a child, and it can also describe a child coming into the world. Thus, its sense depends on whether the sentence presents someone as producing a child or as being born. It is a common word in the Greek Old Testament and related writings, occurring 246 times, especially in genealogical and family records. Its basic idea remains connected with physical descent and the beginning of a person’s life.

This word is a proper name for a place called “Dabirōth” or “Thaviroth.” It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual concept; it identifies a specific location in the Greek Old Testament. The name occurs once, in Joshua 19:12, within the boundary descriptions recorded there. Since the available information does not include the verse text or wider geographical details, the safest meaning is simply the place-name itself, with its alternate English rendering preserved.

This word is a proper name: “Dagōn” or “Thagon.” It identifies Dagon rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books, it occurs 17 times, with most occurrences in 1 Samuel. The name appears in passages from Judges, 1 Samuel, Isaiah, 1 Chronicles, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “leap across,” describing the act of moving over or across something in a single bound. It presents an active movement rather than a state or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Song of Songs 2:8. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the movement, but its central meaning remains a decisive leap across an intervening space.

This adjective means “twofold; double,” describing something that has two parts, twice the amount, or a doubled quality. It functions as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or action. In the Greek text represented here, it occurs twice, both times in Sirach, so its basic sense is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included. The rendering “double” agrees with this central meaning.

This Greek LXX noun refers to discontent or peevishness—a displeased, irritable attitude rather than simple sadness. It names an inward disposition of dissatisfaction or annoyance. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Job 34:30; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here. Its basic meaning points to a troubled attitude that can affect how a person responds to others or to circumstances.

This Greek LXX noun means “number seven.” It identifies the quantity seven and serves as a counting term in passages throughout the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books. It occurs 22 times in this LXX corpus, including passages in Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Daniel, and Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the number seven.

This noun means “putting out; exposing”—bringing something into the open or placing it before others. It describes an act of presentation or disclosure rather than a person, object, or inward feeling. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Daniel and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains the outward setting forth or revealing of something. The word’s two recorded uses belong to these two distinct LXX books.

This Greek LXX verb means to offer willingly or to be willing. It describes a person choosing to give, act, or participate freely rather than being compelled. In the LXX, it appears nine times, chiefly in Judges and Ezra, where the surrounding wording presents willingness as a deliberate response. Its central idea is voluntary readiness: someone makes an offering or takes action with a willing heart. The exact emphasis in any particular verse depends on its surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means to break the vertebrae—the bones forming the backbone. It describes a severe physical act directed against the spine, rather than a general kind of breaking. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 11:18. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative, but its basic meaning is clear: to fracture or break the vertebrae of a person or creature.

Eliel, also rendered Elil, is a personal name identifying an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears six times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, all within Chronicles. Because it functions as a name, its basic meaning is the person designated by that name; the surrounding passage identifies which Eliel is intended in each occurrence. The name appears five times in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Chronicles.

Elphalat, also rendered Elfalat, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 5:16. Because it is a name, its meaning is primarily identifying the person who bears it; the name itself does not provide a broader teaching or concept apart from its appearance in the biblical record.

This noun means “belittling”—treating a person or thing as unworthy, insignificant, or beneath proper regard. It describes an attitude or expression that diminishes someone rather than honoring their value. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs six times, appearing in Psalms, Ezekiel, Wisdom, Sirach, and 2 and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording and subject.

ἔνθα means “there.” It is an adverb that points to a place, directing attention to a location already understood from the sentence or surrounding passage. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times across six verses, including passages in 2 Kings, 1 Maccabees, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its basic function remains straightforward: it identifies a place rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. The precise location it indicates must be understood from the verse and its surrounding context.

This Greek LXX noun means “pipe,” referring to a tube or hollow instrument. It is a specific physical object rather than an action or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament text represented here, at Zechariah 4:2. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included, the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be stated beyond its basic meaning: a pipe or tube. Its lexical meaning is directly identified as “pipe.”

This noun means an “injunction” or “command”—an authoritative instruction given for someone to follow. It refers to a directive rather than a suggestion, emphasizing the obligation carried by the speaker’s words. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 8:6. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and argument, but its basic sense is a command or binding instruction.

This LXX Greek noun means “wool,” the soft fiber obtained from sheep and used as a material for clothing, coverings, or other woven goods. It names a tangible substance rather than an action, quality, or spiritual condition. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages ranging from Deuteronomy and Judges to Psalms, Proverbs, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding verse determines how the wool is being used or described.

This Greek LXX adverb means “favourably,” describing an action done or received in a favorable manner. It points to a positive or gracious disposition rather than naming a person, object, or event. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX, at Wisdom 6:16, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here. Its precise force in that verse depends on the sentence and passage around it.

This adjective describes something as “well-suited”—fitting its purpose or appropriate for the task at hand. It points to practical suitability rather than merely describing appearance or quality in the abstract. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs twice: once in Proverbs and once in Wisdom. Because no verse text is provided here, its precise application in either passage depends on the surrounding context, but its ordinary sense remains clear: something well matched to a need, purpose, or use.

This Greek word means “leader” or “governor,” referring to a person who exercises authority over others. It is a noun used for someone who directs, oversees, or governs a people or territory. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, it occurs 81 times, showing that it commonly describes recognized human authority. The exact responsibilities of such a person depend on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains one who leads or governs.

This Greek LXX adjective means “sweet,” describing something pleasing in taste or agreeable in experience. It can refer to food or drink, but its ordinary meaning can also describe pleasant speech, pleasant results, or something enjoyed by the senses. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented in this corpus, showing use across several kinds of writing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being described, but the central idea remains pleasant sweetness.

gl: one who holds the reins; driver
d: one who holds the reins; driver

e.t: This noun means “one who holds the reins; driver,” referring to the person who controls and guides a vehicle or its animals. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Kings 22:34 and 2 Chronicles 18:33. Its basic sense is practical and specific: a driver or charioteer responsible for directing movement by handling the reins. The surrounding verse determines the exact scene, but the word itself identifies the person performing this driving role.

This adverb describes acting with courage, boldness, or manly resolve—doing something bravely or manfully. It tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, object, or quality by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, all in 3 and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense is courageous and resolute action.

Iabi, also written Iavi, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament text. The name occurs once, in Numbers 13:14, and its precise personal reference belongs to that passage’s surrounding list and context. By itself, the name does not provide a broader definition or spiritual concept; it functions simply as an individual designation. The two forms supplied for the name are Iabi and Iavi.

Iarikam is a proper name—the personal name of an individual identified in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a general quality, action, or common object, but as a distinguishing name. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Joshua 15:56. The available lexical information gives Iarikam as the meaning itself; understanding the person’s role or significance requires the surrounding verse and passage.

Iia is a proper name, referring to a named individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 15:24. The available lexical information identifies the name as “Iia,” but does not provide further meaning or details about the person. Its significance in that verse must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage and the verse’s actual wording.

Isadek is a proper name, also rendered Isathek. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:18. The name itself provides identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the person’s place in that genealogy. Its precise significance therefore lies in whom it names, not in a broader everyday definition.

Ιωδαε is a proper name, represented in English as “Iōdae” or “Iothae.” It functions as a personal name in the Greek Old Testament rather than as a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 57 times across 50 Old Testament verses, especially in Kings and Chronicles. Its precise referent in any passage must be determined from that passage’s surrounding text.

This noun means “covering”—something that covers or conceals another thing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it is used for a covering as a recognizable object or feature, rather than for an action or quality. The word occurs 19 times in this corpus, with appearances in Exodus, Numbers, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on what is being covered and the surrounding context.

Karmēlias, also rendered Karmilias, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Samuel 3:3. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional definition or explanation of its meaning. Its precise reference in that verse belongs to the surrounding passage and verse text, not to the name alone. Thus, this entry should be understood simply as the proper name “Karmēlias; Karmilias.”

This Greek LXX verb means “silent about”: it describes remaining quiet concerning something rather than speaking about it. It is a verb, so it expresses an action or conduct—someone choosing, being caused, or remaining silent in relation to a matter. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Numbers, Nehemiah, and Job. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on what the surrounding sentence identifies as the subject or matter being left unspoken.

This verb means to wound someone severely. It describes an action that causes serious physical injury, rather than a minor hurt or touch. As a verb, it tells what is done to a person or living thing. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 6:6. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: to inflict a severe wound.

This verb means to “herald” or “proclaim”—to make a message known publicly or formally. It describes the act of declaring something so that others hear and recognize the announcement. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 29 times, showing a recurring action rather than a rare or specialized expression. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being proclaimed and to whom, but the central idea remains the public declaration of a message.

This word means “sieve,” a tool used to separate finer material from coarser material. As a noun, it names the physical implement rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 27:4, and its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s basic picture is clear: material passes through an arranged screen, while larger pieces are held back.

Mathani is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in Ezra 10:33. The available lexical information identifies the name simply as “Mathani”; it does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of the name itself. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s role there.

Maron is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Septuagint, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 4:17. The available wording identifies the person simply as Maron, while the surrounding verse text is not included here, so the name itself does not provide further information about his identity or role. Its meaning is therefore the proper name Maron within this Old Testament Greek corpus.

This adjective describes someone or something as “exceeding strong”—strong to an exceptional or surpassing degree. It is a descriptive word rather than the name of an action or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 5:13. The word’s basic sense is clear from its definition, while the surrounding verse would determine exactly what person or thing is being described there.

In the Greek Old Testament, this noun means a “portion”: a share or part belonging to someone or set apart from a larger whole. It can refer to what a person receives, possesses, or has as a designated share, while the exact referent depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs 142 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, including the deuterocanonical books, so it is a broadly used term rather than a rare expression. Its central idea remains an allotted part or share.

gl: pour from one vessel into another; transplant
d: pour from one vessel into another; transplant

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to pour liquid from one vessel into another or to transplant something from one place to another. It describes a deliberate transfer, whether the object is a substance being poured or something living being moved and replanted. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 1:29; its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This noun refers to stands or bases—supporting structures on which something rests. It describes a physical foundation or pedestal rather than an action or abstract idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 20 times, especially in descriptions of the temple furnishings and their construction. The word therefore points to the lower supporting part that bears or steadies another object. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding description.

This Greek Old Testament noun means the upper lip, especially the moustache growing there. It refers to a visible part of the face rather than an action, quality, or abstract idea. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Samuel 19:25. Its precise significance in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a person’s upper lip or moustache. Mōcha is a proper name, also given as “Mokha.” It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an ordinary action, quality, or object. The name occurs four times in the LXX, appearing once in Genesis and three times in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular identity in each passage cannot be described further, but its basic function is that of a personal name.

This word means “swim”: to move through water using the body. It is a verb, so it describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Job 11:12. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the action of swimming or moving through water. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that translation corpus.

Ozom is a proper name preserved in the Greek Old Testament rendering of these genealogical passages. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or theological idea. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament text, both times in 1 Chronicles chapter 2, at 1 Chronicles 2:26 and 2:28. No broader lexical definition is given for Ozom, so its ordinary meaning is simply the personal name “Ozom.”

This adjective describes a person who is “morose”—gloomy or low-spirited in mood. It identifies a condition of inward heaviness rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, in Proverbs and Isaiah, showing that the word can describe a somber disposition in both wisdom teaching and prophetic language. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This adjective describes people who belong to the same race or people-group. It identifies shared ancestry or ethnic identity rather than describing an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense is “of the same race,” and the surrounding sentence determines exactly whom it identifies in each passage.

This word means “not” or “not actually.” It is an adverb used to negate a statement, action, or description, marking something as untrue, rejected, or absent. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 174 times, so it is a common way to express denial or negation. Its precise force in a sentence depends on the words it modifies, but its central function remains clear: it says that something is not so.

gl: look aside; take a side look
d: look aside; take a side look

e.t: This verb means to “look aside” or “take a side look.” It describes directing one’s gaze away from a straight or immediate view, rather than simply looking generally. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times: three times in Job and once each in Sirach and Song of Songs. Its exact force in any verse depends on what the surrounding sentence says about the person looking and what is being viewed.

This Greek LXX word means “five,” referring to a quantity of five persons, objects, or units. It functions as a number and can identify how many are present or being counted. The word appears 250 times in the Greek Old Testament and Greek deuterocanonical corpus, showing regular use in descriptions of families, offerings, arrangements, and measured groups. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning remains the number five.

This Greek LXX verb means “disconnect” or “remove.” It describes taking something away, separating it from what it was attached to, or causing a connection to cease. The word is used 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical writings represented here, so its basic sense applies broadly to physical removal and separation. The surrounding sentence determines exactly what is being removed or disconnected in each passage.

This LXX word means “distraction”: something that draws the mind or attention away and makes sustained thought or purposeful work difficult. It functions as a noun or adjective, so it can describe either the distracting condition or something characterized by it. The word occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical corpus, chiefly in Ecclesiastes. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains divided or diverted attention.

This word means “brick,” a shaped building material used in construction. As a noun, it refers to the individual material itself, whether one brick or several. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 10 times across 9 verses, including passages associated with building and structures. Its ordinary meaning remains concrete and physical rather than symbolic by itself; the surrounding verse determines whether the brick is part of a building description, an object being made, or an image used in a larger statement.

This word means “river,” referring to a natural stream or channel of flowing water. It is a noun used for rivers as recognizable features of the land, whether they mark a journey, supply water, or form part of a place’s setting. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 229 times, showing that this is a well-established and widely used word for a river. Its exact significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and context.

This verb describes choosing something beforehand or making a deliberate choice. It points to an act of purposeful selection rather than a merely accidental or unconsidered decision. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs 11 times across 11 verses, including passages in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Proverbs, and later Jewish writings. Its basic emphasis is the inward act of deciding in advance; the surrounding verse determines what is chosen and why.

e.h: A Vat Before a Wine Press
e.t: This noun means a “vat fronting a wine press”—a container positioned before the press to receive or hold what the press produces. It names a specific part of wine-making equipment rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 5:2, so its meaning is narrowly defined by this direct description rather than by many repeated uses. The word’s basic sense is therefore a physical vat associated with a wine press.

“Assign; attach” is the basic meaning of this Greek LXX verb. It describes giving something a designated place, connection, or association—joining it to someone or something by assignment. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 6:33. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, its precise force in that sentence cannot be described further; the established lexical sense remains the safe guide. It is a compact action word concerned with assigning or attaching, rather than a general term for any kind of relationship.

This word means “face,” referring to the front of a person’s head. It functions as a noun and names a person’s visible countenance or front. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Kings 20:4. Its basic meaning is clear, while the surrounding verse determines whether the face is being mentioned simply as a physical feature or carries a more specific role in the sentence.

This word means “tower”: a raised structure or building identified as a tower. It is a noun, so it names rather than describes an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 68 times, showing regular use for this kind of structure. It appears across many biblical books, from Genesis through Song of Songs. The central meaning remains straightforward, while the significance of a particular tower depends on the surrounding passage.

Rathamin, also written Rhathamin, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The available information identifies the name but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or translation. In the Greek LXX corpus, it appears once, in 1 Maccabees 11:34. Its precise reference may identify its bearer or setting, but that cannot be determined without the verse text and surrounding context.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Rebes” or “Rheves.” It functions as a name rather than a common word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:20. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be identified more specifically here; the available lexical information establishes the name and its use as a proper noun.

Sediour, also rendered Sethiur, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in the book of Numbers. Because it is a proper name, its meaning in a sentence is to identify a particular person; the surrounding passage is needed to determine that person’s role in each occurrence. The name appears from Numbers 1 through Numbers 10.

Seōn, also rendered Sion, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named person or place rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. The name occurs 37 times across 34 verses in the Greek Old Testament, especially in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. Its exact referent in any passage must be determined from the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek LXX noun means “shelter.” It refers to a place, covering, or provision of safety, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word is used 20 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX books, so it describes a recurring idea rather than a rare technical term. In passages where it appears, the surrounding context determines what provides the shelter and who receives its protection.

This Greek LXX noun means “breast” or “chest,” referring to the front upper part of the body. It names a physical body area rather than an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Sirach 26:18. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included, the word’s precise reference in that sentence must be understood from its context. Its basic meaning remains the body’s breast or chest area.

This noun refers to a bed spread, a covering or bedding laid over a bed. It occurs nine times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from Genesis, Esther, Job, Psalms, Ezekiel, and Amos. The word therefore names an ordinary household furnishing rather than an action or abstract idea. Its precise sense in any particular verse is shaped by the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a spread or covering associated with a bed.

This Greek LXX verb means “come together; meet.” It describes people or parties coming into one another’s presence, or joining together. In this corpus, it occurs five times, all in the deuterocanonical books: four times in 2 Maccabees and once in Bel and the Dragon. One English rendering is “meet,” which fits the word’s basic sense. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea is coming together or meeting.

This verb means to dash something to pieces—to break or crush it forcefully. It describes an action that leaves what is struck shattered rather than whole. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, five in Psalms and once in Micah, showing a consistent sense of violent breaking or crushing. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains forceful destruction or fragmentation.

This Greek LXX adverb means “concisely,” describing speech or writing expressed in a brief, compact way rather than at length. It tells how something is said, summarized, or communicated. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here: twice in Proverbs and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on brevity and directness; the surrounding verse determines what particular statement is being expressed concisely.

Tanin is a proper name preserved as “Tanin” in the Greek Old Testament tradition. It does not function as an ordinary descriptive word or action; it identifies a named entity. This name occurs twice in the LXX corpus, once in Numbers 13:22 and once in Ezekiel 30:14. Without the surrounding verse text, the specific person, place, or thing identified by the name cannot be stated more precisely.

Tryphōn is a proper name, rendered as “Tryphōn” or “Trifon.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the name occurs 20 times, all in 1 Maccabees, from 1 Maccabees 11:39 through 15:39. Its exact significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions simply as a personal name.

This word means an aqueduct or conduit—a structure or channel that carries water from one place to another. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament and related writings for a water-supply work, especially one bringing water into or through a city. The word occurs five times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages in 2 Kings and Isaiah. Its basic sense remains concrete: a built waterway or channel, rather than the water itself. The precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “remembrance” or “remembering.” It refers to the act or result of calling something to mind and keeping it in memory. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings: once in Ezra and twice in 2 Maccabees. Its precise emphasis in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea is memory being preserved, recalled, or brought to attention. It is a focused term for remembrance rather than a broad description of knowledge or understanding.

This verb means to assert or claim—to present something as true or make a definite statement about it. It describes what a person says, not necessarily whether the claim is correct; the surrounding passage determines that. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs five times, serving as a direct word for expressing an assertion or stated claim. Its use is verbal: it portrays someone actively declaring or maintaining something.

This Greek LXX noun refers to an expressed sound, especially the way something is voiced: an “enunciation” or “tone.” It points to audible expression rather than merely an unspoken thought. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, once in Psalms and once in Wisdom. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and how the sound is being described. These meanings identify the word’s ordinary sense without assigning a particular emotional or spiritual quality to it.

This Greek LXX verb means “explain”: to make something understood by setting out its meaning or details. It describes an act of clarification rather than merely mentioning something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, in Job and Daniel, so its sense is focused and consistent rather than broad or frequent. The precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding words and passage.

e.h: A Stick or Piece of Wood
e.t: This Greek LXX noun means “stick,” referring to a small piece or slender piece of wood. It can describe dry or gathered wood, such as material that may be scattered, burned, or used as a simple object. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Hosea. Its basic meaning remains concrete and ordinary: a stick or piece of wood rather than an abstract idea.

This word is the proper name “Chanaan,” also rendered “Khanaan.” It functions as a personal or place name rather than as a description, so its meaning is primarily the named designation itself. In the Greek Septuagint corpus, it occurs 94 times, appearing throughout the Old Testament portion and twice in the deuterocanonical books. The name is found from Genesis through 1 Maccabees, showing that it is used consistently as a recognized biblical name.

This word means “flea,” the small jumping insect. It is a noun naming the creature itself, rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Samuel 24:15. The word therefore has a specific, concrete meaning, while the precise force of the reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its English rendering is “flea,” matching the basic lexical sense directly.

Ōbil, also rendered Ovil, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at 1 Chronicles 27:30. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity can be stated, but no further meaning or role should be assigned to the name itself.
